category: PCB board setup, layer stack & design rules
description: Everything that defines the physical and electrical constraints of an Altium PCB before and during layout: the board shape and origin, the Layer Stack Manager with materials, impedance profiles and via spans, the complete design rule system across its eight categories, object classes and rooms, and the online and batch Design Rule Check that enforces them.

tools.name: Board Shape (Define from selected objects / Redefine)
tools.description: Sets the board outline. Design > Board Shape > Define Board Shape from Selected Objects converts selected closed primitives (typically a mechanical-layer outline imported from MCAD) into the board shape; Redefine Board Shape draws it interactively; Create Primitives From Board Shape does the reverse, generating a line loop on a chosen layer. Everything from plane extents to DRC board-outline clearance follows this shape.
tools.usage: Design > Board Shape > Redefine Board Shape / Define Board Shape from Selected Objects / Create Primitives From Board Shape / Move Board Vertices
tools.example: Import the MCAD DXF onto Mechanical 1, select the closed outline, Design > Board Shape > Define Board Shape from Selected Objects.
tools.notes: Prefer driving the shape from a mechanical layer outline so that re-importing an updated MCAD outline is a two-click operation.

tools.name: Board cutouts and board regions
tools.description: Holes and shaped openings inside the board are created as board cutouts — a polygon drawn on the board and converted with Tools > Convert > Create Board Cutout from selected primitives. In rigid-flex designs, board regions instead subdivide the shape into areas with different layer stacks.
tools.usage: Draw a closed shape > Tools > Convert > Create Board Cutout from Selected Primitives; rigid-flex: Design > Layer Stack Manager > board regions / Design > Define Board Region
tools.example: Draw a rectangle where the display window must pass through, select it, Tools > Convert > Create Board Cutout from Selected Primitives.

tools.name: Layer Stack Manager
tools.description: Defines the board's construction: signal, plane, dielectric, solder mask and overlay layers in order, each with material, thickness, copper weight, dielectric constant and loss tangent. It also owns the drill (via span) table, impedance profiles and, for rigid-flex, multiple stackups assigned to board regions. It is opened as its own document tab so it can be edited alongside the board.
tools.usage: Design > Layer Stack Manager… (opens the .PcbDoc's stackup editor tab)

parameters.name: Layer / Material / Thickness
parameters.description: Physical construction, driving total thickness, impedance and 3D rendering.

parameters.name: Dk / Df
parameters.description: Dielectric constant and dissipation factor used by the impedance calculator and signal-integrity tools.

parameters.name: Impedance tab
parameters.description: Named impedance profiles (single-ended and differential) that compute the trace width and gap needed for a target impedance.

parameters.name: Via types (drill pairs)
parameters.description: Through, blind, buried and micro via spans available to the router.

parameters.name: Back drilling
parameters.description: Per-drill-pair back-drill definition to remove unused via stub.

tools.example: Design > Layer Stack Manager > add two internal planes > Impedance tab > new profile 'Z50' targeting 50 Ω on Top with a 0.2 mm prepreg — Altium reports the required trace width.
tools.notes: Assign impedance profiles to nets through the Width rule's impedance option so the router uses the calculated width automatically.

tools.name: View Configuration panel (layers & colours)
tools.description: Controls what is visible and how it is drawn: per-layer visibility and colour, layer sets, 2D and 3D view options, system colours, grids, and the transparency and rendering settings for 3D bodies. Layer sets (e.g. 'Top Routing', 'Assembly') switch large groups of layers at once.
tools.usage: View > Panels > View Configuration (shortcut L in the PCB editor opens the layer view configuration)
tools.example: Press L, create a layer set 'Mech only' showing just the mechanical layers, and switch to it while checking the enclosure fit.

tools.name: Layer Sets
tools.description: Named collections of layers that can be made visible, active or printable together. Beyond convenience they are used by the layer-pair navigation in rigid-flex and multi-layer boards, and by output configurations that need to print a consistent set of layers.
tools.usage: View Configuration panel > Layer Sets dropdown > Add/Manage Layer Sets
tools.example: Create the set 'DDR route' containing Top, GND1, Signal2 and the associated mechanical layers, then switch to it while routing memory.

tools.name: Mechanical layers and layer pairs
tools.description: Mechanical layers carry non-electrical data: board outline, MCAD geometry, assembly drawing, courtyards, glue dots, fabrication notes, dimensions. Each can be given a layer type (Assembly Top, Courtyard Top, Component Center, Dimensions, 3D Body …) so that Altium's outputs and checks know its purpose, and layer pairs tie a top layer to its bottom counterpart so flipping a component moves its mechanical data to the right side.
tools.usage: Design > Layer Stack Manager > Mechanical layers; layer pairs configured in the same editor / View Configuration
tools.example: Set Mechanical 13/29 as an Assembly Top/Bottom pair so that flipping a footprint moves its assembly outline correctly.
tools.notes: Assigning the proper layer type is what lets Draftsman, the 3D view and the output generators pick the right layers automatically.

tools.name: Design Rules dialog
tools.description: The single dialog holding every design rule, organised in eight categories: Electrical, Routing, SMT, Mask, Plane, Testpoint, Manufacturing, High Speed, Placement and Signal Integrity. Each rule has a name, a priority, an enable flag, one or two scopes written as query expressions, and its constraint values. The most specific matching rule of a category wins, resolved by priority.
tools.usage: Design > Rules… (D,R)

parameters.name: Where The First Object Matches
parameters.description: Query scope, from simple pickers (All, Net, Net Class, Layer, Net and Layer) or a custom query.

parameters.name: Priority
parameters.description: Order in which rules of the same category are tested; Priorities… button reorders them.

parameters.name: Constraints
parameters.description: The rule's actual values, which differ per rule type.

tools.example: Design > Rules > Electrical > Clearance > New Rule; scope `InNetClass('POWER')` versus `All`, clearance 0.4 mm, priority 1.
tools.notes: Design Rule Checker reports which rule actually applied; use the PCB Rules and Violations panel or Board Insight to see the winning rule for a given object.

tools.name: Clearance rule
tools.description: The primary electrical spacing rule: minimum gap between objects of different nets, with an optional matrix giving a different clearance for each object-kind pair (track-to-pad, pad-to-pad, via-to-via, SMD-to-SMD…). Multiple clearance rules with net-class scopes implement creepage and high-voltage spacing alongside a tighter default.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Electrical > Clearance
tools.example: Default clearance 0.15 mm for All-All; a second rule scoped `InNetClass('MAINS')` to `All` with 6 mm, priority 1.

tools.name: Short-Circuit and Un-Routed Net rules
tools.description: Short-Circuit decides whether objects of different nets are allowed to touch (normally not, but it is deliberately allowed between, say, two ground nets joined at a single point). Un-Routed Net flags connections that have no complete copper path, which is the rule that makes the DRC report tell you the board is not finished.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Electrical > Short-Circuit / Un-Routed Net / Un-Connected Pin
tools.example: Add a Short-Circuit rule scoped `InNet('AGND')` to `InNet('DGND')` with 'Allow Short Circuit' ticked so the single-point tie is legal.

tools.name: Width rule
tools.description: Sets minimum, preferred and maximum track width per scope, optionally per layer and optionally derived from an impedance profile in the Layer Stack Manager. The interactive router starts at the preferred width and refuses to go outside min/max, so this rule is what drives sensible default widths for power, signal and controlled-impedance nets.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Routing > Width

parameters.name: Min / Preferred / Max Width
parameters.description: Bounds and default used by interactive routing.

parameters.name: Layers in layerstack
parameters.description: Per-layer overrides so an inner layer can use a different width.

parameters.name: Use impedance profile
parameters.description: Derives the width from a named impedance profile instead of a fixed number.

tools.example: Rule 'PowerWidth', scope `InNetClass('POWER')`, Min 0.5 / Preferred 0.8 / Max 2 mm, priority above the default Width rule.

tools.name: Routing Topology, Priority, Layers and Corners rules
tools.description: Shape the router's behaviour. Routing Topology sets how a multi-pin net is connected (Shortest, Horizontal, Vertical, Daisy-Simple, Daisy-MidDriven, Daisy-Balanced, Starburst), which changes the ratsnest and is essential for terminated buses. Routing Priority orders which nets are routed first, Routing Layers enables or forbids layers per net, and Routing Corners sets the corner style and setback.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Routing > Routing Topology / Routing Priority / Routing Layers / Routing Corners
tools.example: Set Routing Topology to 'Daisy-MidDriven' on the memory clock net so the ratsnest reflects the intended fly-by topology.

tools.name: Routing Via Style rule
tools.description: Defines the via diameter and hole size (min/preferred/max) used when the interactive router places a via, per scope. Separate rules give power nets bigger vias than signals, and micro-via scopes drive HDI designs. Together with the Layer Stack's drill pairs it decides which via types the router may use.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Routing > Routing Via Style
tools.example: Rule 'PowerVia', scope `InNetClass('POWER')`, Via diameter 0.8 mm / hole 0.4 mm; default signal via 0.45/0.25 mm.

tools.name: Differential Pairs Routing rule
tools.description: Constrains a differential pair's geometry: minimum, maximum and preferred gap and width, maximum uncoupled length, and optionally an impedance profile that derives both. The interactive differential pair router obeys it, and the DRC flags pairs that exceed the uncoupled length at breakouts.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Routing > Differential Pairs Routing; pairs themselves are created in the PCB panel's Differential Pairs Editor
tools.example: Rule scoped `InDifferentialPairClass('USB')`, Min/Preferred/Max gap 0.12/0.15/0.2 mm, Max Uncoupled Length 5 mm.

tools.name: Fanout Control rule
tools.description: Governs the automatic fanout of SMD pads to vias: the fanout style (Auto, Inline Rows, Staggered Rows, BGA, Under Pads), the direction (In Only, Out Only, Alternating…), and the via placement mode. It is what makes Route > Fanout produce a usable BGA escape pattern rather than random vias.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Routing > Fanout Control (separate defaults for BGA, LCC, SOIC, Small and Default)
tools.example: Set the BGA fanout rule to style 'BGA', direction 'Alternating In/Out', Via Placement Mode 'Close To Pad', then run Route > Fanout > Component.

tools.name: SMT rules (SMD To Corner / To Plane / Neck-Down)
tools.description: Control how a track leaves an SMD pad: SMD To Corner sets the minimum straight run before the first corner, SMD To Plane the distance to a plane connection point, and SMD Neck-Down the percentage by which a track may narrow at the pad. They prevent acid traps and solder-wicking geometry at fine-pitch parts.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > SMT > SMD To Corner / SMD To Plane / SMD Neck-Down / Component Body Clearance
tools.example: SMD To Corner 0.25 mm on the 0.4 mm-pitch QFN so tracks run straight out of the pad before turning.

tools.name: Mask rules (Solder Mask / Paste Mask Expansion)
tools.description: Set how far the solder mask opening and the paste stencil aperture extend beyond (or inside, with a negative value) the copper pad, per scope. Paste mask reduction on large thermal pads and windowed mask on fine-pitch parts are both configured here rather than by editing every footprint.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Mask > Solder Mask Expansion / Paste Mask Expansion
tools.example: Solder Mask Expansion 0.05 mm globally; a second Paste Mask Expansion rule of -0.1 mm scoped to the QFN thermal pad.

tools.name: Plane rules (Power Plane Connect Style, Clearance, Polygon Connect)
tools.description: Define how pads and vias attach to copper planes and polygons. Power Plane Connect Style chooses Relief Connect (with conductor width, count and air gap), Direct Connect or No Connect; Power Plane Clearance sets the anti-pad around a non-connected hole; Polygon Connect Style does the same for polygon pours, including the thermal spoke angle.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Plane > Power Plane Connect Style / Power Plane Clearance / Polygon Connect Style

parameters.name: Connect Style
parameters.description: Relief Connect, Direct Connect or No Connect.

parameters.name: Conductors / Conductor Width / Air Gap
parameters.description: Thermal spoke count, spoke width and the gap around the pad.

parameters.name: Angle
parameters.description: 45° or 90° spokes for polygon thermal reliefs.

tools.example: Polygon Connect Style: Relief Connect, 4 conductors, 0.3 mm wide, 0.25 mm air gap, 45° — but Direct Connect for the scope `InNetClass('POWER')` on the heatsink pad.

tools.name: Testpoint rules (Fabrication and Assembly)
tools.description: Two rule families — Fabrication Testpoint Style/Usage and Assembly Testpoint Style/Usage — define what qualifies as a test point (size, grid, layer, whether vias and component pads count, tented or not) and which nets require one. The Testpoint Manager then generates and reports them.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Testpoint > Fabrication Testpoint Style / Usage, Assembly Testpoint Style / Usage; Tools > Testpoint Manager
tools.example: Fabrication Testpoint Style: min size 0.9 mm, grid 1.27 mm, bottom side, allow vias; Usage: Required for all nets. Then Tools > Testpoint Manager > Auto Assign.

tools.name: Manufacturing rules
tools.description: The DFM family: Minimum Annular Ring, Acute Angle, Hole Size, Layer Pairs, Hole To Hole Clearance, Minimum Solder Mask Sliver, Silk To Solder Mask Clearance, Silk To Silk Clearance, Net Antennae, Board Outline Clearance and (in newer releases) silkscreen-over-component-pad checks. These are the rules a fabricator's capability sheet translates into.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Manufacturing > (Minimum Annular Ring, Acute Angle, Hole Size, Layer Pairs, Hole To Hole Clearance, Minimum Solder Mask Sliver, Silk To Solder Mask Clearance, Silk to Silk Clearance, Net Antennae, Board Outline Clearance)
tools.example: Minimum Annular Ring 0.15 mm, Hole Size min 0.2 / max 6.3 mm, Hole To Hole Clearance 0.25 mm, Silk To Solder Mask Clearance 0.1 mm — taken straight from the fab's capability table.
tools.notes: Set these from the chosen fabricator's published capabilities before routing, not after: they change minimum via sizes and therefore the whole escape strategy.

tools.name: High Speed rules
tools.description: The timing and integrity family: Parallel Segment (coupled-length limits for crosstalk), Length (min/max net length), Matched Lengths (group tolerance with tuning), Daisy Chain Stub Length, Vias Under SMD, Maximum Via Count and Return Path. They are the constraints the length-tuning tools and the DRC use to police high-speed buses.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > High Speed > Parallel Segment / Length / Matched Lengths / Daisy Chain Stub Length / Vias Under SMD / Maximum Via Count / Return Path

parameters.name: Matched Lengths > Tolerance
parameters.description: Allowed spread within the matched group, used by the interactive length tuner's gauge.

parameters.name: Parallel Segment
parameters.description: For a given gap, the maximum parallel run length before a violation.

parameters.name: Return Path
parameters.description: Flags traces whose adjacent reference plane is interrupted.

tools.example: Matched Lengths rule scoped `InNetClass('DDR_DQ0')` with tolerance 0.2 mm; Parallel Segment: for gap < 0.2 mm, limit 10 mm.

tools.name: xSignals
tools.description: Defines a timing path that spans several nets through series components — for example MCU pin, series resistor, connector, memory pin — as one length-matchable entity. Without xSignals, length rules only see individual nets and matching across a series termination is impossible. The xSignal Wizard generates them automatically for memory interfaces.
tools.usage: Design > xSignals > Create xSignals From Connected Nets / Run the xSignal Wizard; manage in the PCB panel's xSignals view
tools.example: Design > xSignals > xSignal Wizard > select the MCU and the DDR chip > generate xSignals per byte lane > apply a Matched Lengths rule to the generated xSignal classes.
tools.notes: Length tuning gauges read xSignal lengths, so create them before tuning any interface that passes through series resistors.

tools.name: Placement rules (Room Definition, Component Clearance, Component Orientations, Height)
tools.description: Constrain where and how components sit: Room Definition binds a component class to a rectangular room on a side and layer; Component Clearance sets the minimum body-to-body gap (checked against courtyards or bounding boxes); Height limits component height in a scope; Permitted Layers and Nets to Ignore complete the family.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Placement > Room Definition / Component Clearance / Component Orientations / Permitted Layers / Nets to Ignore / Height
tools.example: Height rule scoped `WithinRoom('UnderShield')` with maximum 1.6 mm so nothing taller than the can is placed there.

tools.name: Signal Integrity rules
tools.description: Targets for the built-in signal-integrity analyser: Signal Stimulus, Overshoot and Undershoot (rising and falling), Impedance, Signal Top Value, Signal Base Value, Flight Time, Slope and Supply Nets. They let the SI analysis report pass/fail against explicit limits instead of raw waveforms.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > Signal Integrity > (Signal Stimulus, Overshoot/Undershoot Rising/Falling Edge, Impedance, Signal Top/Base Value, Flight Time Rising/Falling Edge, Slope Rising/Falling Edge, Supply Nets)
tools.example: Set Supply Nets (+3V3 = 3.3 V, GND = 0 V) and Overshoot Rising Edge 0.33 V, then run Tools > Signal Integrity.

tools.name: Design Rule Checker (batch DRC)
tools.description: Runs every enabled rule over the whole board and produces an HTML/text report plus violation markers. The dialog's Rules To Check page enables each rule for Online and/or Batch checking independently, and the Report Options page controls whether violations are also created as objects so they appear in the PCB Rules and Violations panel.
tools.usage: Tools > Design Rule Check… (T,D)

parameters.name: Online / Batch
parameters.description: Per-rule flags: Online checks while editing, Batch checks only when the DRC is run.

parameters.name: Create Report File
parameters.description: Writes the Design Rule Verification Report.

parameters.name: Create Violations
parameters.description: Adds violation objects to the board so they can be browsed and cleared.

parameters.name: Stop when N violations found
parameters.description: Prevents a runaway report on a board with a badly scoped rule.

tools.example: Tools > Design Rule Check > Rules To Check > enable all Manufacturing rules for Batch > Run Design Rule Check; open the report and work through the violations.
tools.notes: Online DRC catches most problems as you work; always finish with a batch DRC, because several manufacturing and high-speed checks are batch-only by default.

tools.name: PCB Rules and Violations panel
tools.description: Browses the rule system from the results end: it lists rule classes, the individual rules and every current violation, with cross-probing to the offending objects and the ability to jump straight to the rule that was broken. It is the fastest way to work through a DRC report without leaving the board.
tools.usage: View > Panels > PCB Rules And Violations
tools.example: Open the panel, expand 'Clearance Constraint', click a violation — the board zooms to the two objects and the offending rule is identified.

tools.name: Rule Wizard
tools.description: Steps through creating a rule when the query syntax is unfamiliar: choose the rule type, build the scope from pickers (whole board, net, net class, layer, component class, footprint), set the priority relative to existing rules, and enter the constraints. It writes the same query a hand-edited rule would.
tools.usage: Design > Rules > (right-click a rule category) > Rule Wizard…
tools.example: Rule Wizard > Clearance > scope 'A Net Class' = HV > constraint 8 mm > priority 1.

tools.name: Query Builder / query language
tools.description: The expression language behind rule scopes, the PCB and SCH filters, the List panel and output filters. Functions include `InNet('…')`, `InNetClass('…')`, `InComponent('…')`, `InComponentClass('…')`, `OnLayer('…')`, `WithinRoom('…')`, `HasFootprint('…')`, `IsPad`, `IsVia`, `IsTrack`, `IsPolygon`, combined with And/Or/Not and comparison operators. The Query Helper provides a categorised list with a syntax check.
tools.usage: Any rule scope or filter box > Query Helper / Query Builder button
tools.example:
InNetClass('DDR_DQ') And OnLayer('Top Layer') And IsTrack
Not IsTestPoint And IsVia And (HoleSize < 0.3mm)

tools.name: Object Class Explorer
tools.description: Creates and edits the classes that rule scopes target: net classes, component classes, layer classes, pad classes, from-to classes, differential pair classes, design channel classes and xSignal classes. Classes can be created manually here or generated automatically from the schematic by Project Options > Class Generation.
tools.usage: Design > Classes… (D,C)
tools.example: Design > Classes > Net Classes > Add Class 'POWER' > move +3V3, +5V, VBUS and GND into it; every power-related rule can now be scoped with InNetClass('POWER').

tools.name: Net classes from the schematic
tools.description: Project Options > Class Generation automatically creates PCB net classes from buses and from Parameter Set directives, and component classes and rooms from sheets, so the classification is maintained in the schematic where the engineer works. Schematic-defined rules (a Parameter Set carrying `Rule = Width(...)`) travel across in the same ECO.
tools.usage: Project > Project Options > Class Generation; place Parameter Set directives on the schematic for rules
tools.example: Tick 'Generate Net Classes' for buses; after the ECO the PCB has a net class per bus ready for a Width and Matched Lengths rule.

tools.name: Rooms
tools.description: Rectangular or polygonal regions that bind a group of components to an area of the board. Rooms are created automatically per schematic sheet (Class Generation) or manually, and are enforced by the Room Definition placement rule. Design > Rooms offers commands to copy room formats, arrange components inside a room, wrap a room around its components and move a room with its contents.
tools.usage: Design > Rooms > Place Rectangular Room / Place Polygonal Room / Copy Room Formats / Move Room / Wrap Rooms Around Components / Arrange Components Within Room
tools.example: Design > Rooms > Wrap Rooms Around Components on the freshly imported channels, then Copy Room Formats to replicate channel 1's placement into channels 2-8.

tools.name: Board Options / Properties (grids, units, origin)
tools.description: The PCB document's own settings, edited in the Properties panel with nothing selected: measurement unit (mm/mils), the snap grid and component grid, snap options (grids, guides, axes, objects, object hotspots), the board's sheet, and the Board Insight display options. Correct snap settings are what make routing land exactly on pad centres.
tools.usage: Click empty board space > Properties panel (Board, Grid Manager, Guide Manager, Other, Snap Options)
tools.example: Properties > Units: mm, Snap Grid 0.05 mm, tick Snap To Object Hotspots with a 0.2 mm range.

tools.name: Grid Manager (Cartesian and polar grids)
tools.description: Defines multiple named grids — Cartesian or polar — each with its own step, origin, rotation and display style, optionally scoped to a region or a component so a BGA can use its own 0.8 mm grid while the rest of the board uses 0.05 mm. Polar grids make circular LED rings and rotary layouts straightforward.
tools.usage: Properties panel (no selection) > Grid Manager > Add > Cartesian Grid / Polar Grid
tools.example: Grid Manager > Add Polar Grid, centre on the board origin, 24 angular steps and 5 mm radial step, then place the LED ring on it.

tools.name: Set Origin (relative origin)
tools.description: Sets the user origin against which all coordinates are reported and against which outputs (Gerber, drill, pick-and-place) are referenced. Placing it at a defined feature — usually a board corner or a tooling hole — is what makes the manufacturing data unambiguous.
tools.usage: Edit > Origin > Set / Reset
tools.example: Edit > Origin > Set, snap to the bottom-left tooling hole; every output now uses that point as (0,0).

tools.name: Board Insight (heads-up display, mask and dim)
tools.description: The live information overlay on the PCB: a heads-up display near the cursor showing the object under it, its net, layer, size and the applicable rules; single-layer mode; and the mask/dim controls that fade everything except the current selection or net. Shift+H toggles the heads-up display, Shift+S cycles single-layer mode and the Board Insight lens magnifies a region.
tools.usage: Shift+H (heads-up), Shift+S (single layer mode), Shift+X (lens); configured in Preferences > PCB Editor > Board Insight Display / Modes / Colour Overrides
tools.example: Hover over a track with Shift+H on — the HUD reports the net, layer, width and the Width rule that applies to it.

tools.name: Layer visibility and single-layer mode
tools.description: The everyday way to see what matters: the layer tabs at the bottom switch the active layer, Shift+S cycles single-layer modes (hide others, grey others), Ctrl+click a layer tab isolates it, and the L shortcut opens the full layer/colour configuration. On a dense multi-layer board this is the difference between readable and unusable.
tools.usage: Layer tabs / + and - to change layer, Shift+S single layer mode, L for View Configuration
tools.example: Press Shift+S twice to grey every layer except the active one while routing an inner layer.

tools.name: Design Rule Check report (Design Rule Verification Report)
tools.description: The HTML report the batch DRC writes into the project's output folder, listing every rule that was checked, its scope and constraint, and each violation with the objects involved and their coordinates. It is the artefact that goes into a design review or a release package as evidence that the board was checked.
tools.usage: Produced by Tools > Design Rule Check with 'Create Report File' ticked; also available as a Validation output in an OutJob
tools.example: Add 'Design Rule Check' as a Validation output in the release OutJob so a report is generated and stored with every release.
